subtopic_detail: Limits of confidentiality when a specific threat is made to an identifiable person
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 29 year old man in the community clinic. He stopped his risperidone six weeks ago and has slept poorly since.

He tells you that the man in the flat below is transmitting signals into his head through the ceiling and that he has worked out this will only stop if the neighbour is dealt with. He names the neighbour, describes his work hours, and says he bought a hunting knife last week and has it in his kitchen drawer. He is not intoxicated. He asks you to keep what he has told you between the two of you because his mother would be upset, and he declines admission and declines to restart medication.

data_table.Examination: Suspicious and guarded, persecutory delusions with a passivity phenomenon, no cognitive impairment, no intoxication, expressed intent with an identified means and a named target
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines and cannabis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Respect his request and document the threat carefully in the clinical record
options.rationale: Confidentiality yields where there is a serious and imminent threat to the life or safety of an identifiable person, and documentation alone leaves that person unprotected (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines; Privacy Act Australian Privacy Principles).

options.text: Telephone the neighbour yourself to warn him before taking any other step
options.rationale: Warning the person at risk may form part of a proportionate response, but doing it first leaves the patient unassessed in the community with the means still in his kitchen (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange urgent involuntary assessment and inform police of the specific threat
options.rationale: Containment and treatment of the untreated psychosis under mental health legislation is the intervention that reduces the risk, and disclosure limited to the specific threat is permitted where it is necessary to lessen a serious threat to another person's life (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines; Privacy Act Australian Privacy Principles).

options.text: Seek his written consent to disclose before contacting anyone about the threat
options.rationale: Consent should be sought where practicable, but a refusal cannot veto disclosure when the threat is serious, specific and imminent (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

options.text: Restart oral risperidone today and bring him back to the clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: A prescription he has already refused, with review in 24 hours, does nothing about tonight and relies on adherence from a man who stopped treatment six weeks ago (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Confidentiality is a strong but not absolute obligation, and Australian privacy law permits use or disclosure of health information where the clinician reasonably believes it is necessary to lessen or prevent a serious threat to the life, health or safety of any individual. The threshold is judged on specificity, identifiability of the target, expressed intent, available means and the person's history, and this presentation satisfies all of them. Disclosure should be proportionate, meaning the minimum information necessary to the people who need it, rather than a general release of the clinical record. Treating the untreated psychosis is the intervention that actually reduces risk, so the legal and the clinical responses run together rather than as alternatives. Documenting the reasoning, including what was disclosed and to whom and why, is part of the standard.
key_points: Privacy law permits disclosure to lessen a serious threat to life or safety
Specificity, an identifiable target, intent and means raise the threat above the threshold
Disclose the minimum information to those who need it
Treating the underlying psychosis is what reduces the risk
Record the reasoning, the recipients and the content of any disclosure
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the person has acquired a means and where it is kept, because a named target combined with a means already obtained is what converts a general threat into one that requires disclosure that day.

subtopic_detail: Which legal instrument authorises treatment of a physical illness in a patient who lacks capacity
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 78 year old man admitted with a community acquired pneumonia. He has severe depression with psychotic features and is already an involuntary patient under mental health legislation for that illness.

He is refusing intravenous antibiotics. When you assess him he tells you that his lungs rotted away years ago, that he has no blood left in his body, and that treatment is pointless because he is already dead. He cannot repeat back or weigh any of the information you give him about the infection or the consequences of not treating it, and his account does not change when the information is repeated. His oxygen saturation is 89 per cent on room air. There is no advance care directive and his daughter is available and is his nominated substitute decision maker.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 89 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Nihilistic delusions, psychomotor retardation, unable to retain or weigh information about the infection, oriented to person only
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 180 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to authorise the antibiotic treatment?

options.text: Treat under the existing involuntary order because he is already detained
options.rationale: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for the mental illness, and it does not extend to treatment of an unrelated physical illness (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines; Australian Guardianship Legislation).

options.text: Accept his refusal and document that he has declined treatment for pneumonia
options.rationale: A refusal only binds when the person has capacity for that decision, and he cannot retain or weigh the relevant information because of his delusional beliefs (Source: Australian Guardianship Legislation).

options.text: Apply to a tribunal for a guardianship order before giving any antibiotic
options.rationale: A tribunal application is the pathway when no substitute decision maker exists or there is dispute, and the delay is not justifiable when one is available and the patient is hypoxic (Source: Australian Guardianship Legislation).

options.text: Sedate him and give the antibiotics under restraint as an emergency measure
options.rationale: Restraint is a last resort for immediate danger, and reaching for it when a lawful consent pathway is available is neither necessary nor proportionate (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

options.text: Obtain consent from his substitute decision maker after documenting incapacity
options.rationale: Treatment of a physical illness in an adult who lacks capacity is authorised by consent from the substitute decision maker, and the documented capacity assessment is what makes that consent lawful (Source: Australian Guardianship Legislation; RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Two separate legal frameworks operate side by side in this situation and are frequently confused. Mental health legislation permits detention and treatment of the mental illness itself, while consent for treatment of a physical illness in an adult who lacks capacity comes from guardianship legislation through a substitute decision maker, an enduring guardian or a tribunal. Capacity is decision specific and time specific, so a person may lack capacity to decide about antibiotics while retaining it for other choices, and the assessment must show which of the four elements is failing: understanding, retention, weighing or communicating. Nihilistic delusions of the kind described interfere with weighing rather than with understanding, and that distinction is what should be recorded. Emergency treatment can always be given without consent when it is immediately necessary to save life, and that provision covers the interval while the substitute decision maker is contacted.
key_points: Mental health orders do not authorise treatment of unrelated physical illness
Capacity is decision specific and time specific
Record which element of capacity is impaired and why
Substitute decision makers consent for physical treatment when capacity is absent
Emergency life saving treatment may proceed while consent is being obtained
explanation.pearls: A patient detained under mental health legislation retains the ordinary right to consent to or refuse physical health care, so the order in the notes never answers the question of who consents to the antibiotic.

subtopic_detail: Visible haematuria coinciding with an upper respiratory infection in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old man whose urine turned the colour of cola yesterday. He had a sore throat the day before it started and has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each settling within a few days.

He has no dysuria, no flank pain, no rash and no joint symptoms, and he has never smoked. He takes no medication and there is no family history of kidney disease or deafness. His blood pressure today is 142 over 90 on two readings, and he has no oedema. His throat is mildly injected with no exudate and no cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 142/90, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: No rash, no peripheral oedema, no joint swelling, mildly injected pharynx without exudate
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; urine protein creatinine ratio 82 mg/mmol (less than 15); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110); complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the throat with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and repeat the urine later
options.rationale: Antibiotic treatment of the pharyngitis does not alter the glomerular process, and the near simultaneous onset with the sore throat is itself the clue that this is not a post infectious illness (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Refer to nephrology for renal biopsy and formal glomerular assessment
options.rationale: Dysmorphic red cells with casts identify a glomerular source, and the combination of proteinuria above 50 mg/mmol with hypertension is the accepted trigger for biopsy to establish the diagnosis and guide immunosuppression (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography urography and cystoscopy to exclude a tumour
options.rationale: Urological imaging pursues a non glomerular source and is indicated for painless visible haematuria in an older patient with isotropic red cells, not when casts and proteinuria point to the glomerulus (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Reassure him that this follows infection and recheck the urine in six weeks
options.rationale: Post streptococcal disease follows the infection by one to three weeks and is accompanied by a low C3 and a rising antistreptolysin O titre, and neither pattern is present here (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Start perindopril for the blood pressure and review the urine in three months
options.rationale: Blockade of the renin angiotensin system will be part of his long term treatment, but starting it as the whole plan leaves the underlying glomerular disease undiagnosed and unstaged (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

explanation.summary: The first branch point in haematuria is glomerular versus non glomerular, and it is settled by urine microscopy rather than by imaging: dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and proteinuria indicate the glomerulus. Visible haematuria arising within a day or two of a mucosal infection is the hallmark of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, and it is distinguished from post streptococcal glomerulonephritis by the latency, which is one to three weeks there, and by the normal complement here. Prognosis is determined by proteinuria, blood pressure and renal function at presentation rather than by the number of visible bleeding episodes, and biopsy provides the histological scoring that predicts progression. Long term management centres on blood pressure control, blockade of the renin angiotensin system and reduction of proteinuria, with immunosuppression reserved for defined higher risk groups.
key_points: Dysmorphic red cells and casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Haematuria within a day or two of a sore throat suggests immunoglobulin A nephropathy
Post streptococcal disease has a one to three week latency and a low C3
Proteinuria, blood pressure and creatinine at presentation drive prognosis
Urological imaging is for non glomerular bleeding
explanation.pearls: Proteinuria sustained above 1 g per day despite maximal blockade of the renin angiotensin system is the threshold at which immunosuppression is considered in immunoglobulin A nephropathy, which is why quantifying protein at diagnosis matters more than counting bleeding episodes.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic sparing management of uncomplicated acute diverticulitis
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 58 year old woman with two days of steady left iliac fossa pain and a change to looser stool. She has no vomiting and is eating and drinking normally.

She has no diabetes, takes no immunosuppressant or corticosteroid, and has had one similar episode four years ago that settled. On examination her abdomen is soft with localised tenderness in the left iliac fossa, no guarding, no rebound and no palpable mass. Computed tomography of the abdomen reports sigmoid diverticula with pericolic fat stranding and mural thickening, with no abscess, no free gas and no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.5
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with localised left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding or rebound, no mass, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5); computed tomography shows uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis with no abscess, perforation or obstruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with analgesia, oral fluids and review in 48 to 72 hours
options.rationale: Randomised evidence shows no benefit from antibiotics in immunocompetent patients with computed tomography confirmed uncomplicated disease and no systemic sepsis, so supportive care with defined review is the recommended course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; GESA Diverticular Disease).

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for five days and review her then
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are reserved for patients with systemic features, immunosuppression or significant comorbidity, and routine use has not been shown to speed recovery or prevent complications (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole with bowel rest
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy and admission are for complicated disease with abscess or perforation, or for patients who cannot maintain oral intake, and she is well and eating (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange colonoscopy during this admission to inspect the sigmoid segment
options.rationale: Endoscopy during acute inflammation carries a higher perforation risk, and the interval examination to exclude an underlying tumour is scheduled six to eight weeks after resolution (Source: GESA Diverticular Disease).

options.text: Refer for elective sigmoid colectomy after this second documented episode
options.rationale: Elective resection is an individualised decision based on symptom burden, complications and fitness rather than an automatic consequence of a set number of episodes (Source: GESA Diverticular Disease).

explanation.summary: Management of acute diverticulitis has shifted substantially, and the modern first question is whether the episode is uncomplicated on imaging and whether the patient has any feature that puts them outside the trial populations. Immunosuppression, significant comorbidity, systemic sepsis, inability to tolerate oral intake and lack of access to review all push towards antibiotics and admission. In everyone else, analgesia with clear instructions on what should prompt return performs as well as antibiotics without the harms of unnecessary treatment. Colonoscopy is arranged six to eight weeks after resolution when the segment has not been examined recently, because a small proportion of apparent diverticulitis is a perforated carcinoma. Elective resection is a shared decision rather than a fixed rule after a given number of attacks.
key_points: Antibiotics are not required for uncomplicated diverticulitis in a well immunocompetent patient
Immunosuppression or systemic features move the patient into antibiotic treatment
Explicit return advice replaces the antibiotic prescription as the safety net
Interval colonoscopy at six to eight weeks excludes an underlying malignancy
Elective resection is individualised, not triggered by episode count
explanation.pearls: Arrange interval colonoscopy six to eight weeks after an episode of acute diverticulitis unless the colon has been examined within the past year, because a small but real proportion of these presentations turn out to be a perforated colonic carcinoma.

subtopic_detail: Antiviral window and adjunctive decisions in acute herpes zoster
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old man who noticed a painful band of blisters across the right side of his back and flank yesterday morning. A deep burning pain in the same area preceded the rash by three days and is now severe enough to keep him awake.

He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and he takes no immunosuppressant. On examination there are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a single band on the right, extending from the spine to the midline of the abdomen and stopping abruptly at the midline. No lesions are present elsewhere, his face and eyes are unaffected, and he is systemically well with clear lungs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Grouped vesicles on erythematous base in a single unilateral band stopping at the midline, no facial or ocular involvement, no disseminated lesions
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 8.4 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); glycated haemoglobin 52 mmol/mol (less than 48)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply topical aciclovir cream five times daily with simple oral analgesia
options.rationale: Topical antiviral does not achieve therapeutic tissue levels in the affected ganglion and dermatome and has no role in the treatment of shingles (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to cover secondary bacterial infection
options.rationale: Antibacterial cover is added only if there is genuine secondary infection with spreading erythema and purulence, and the vesicles here are typical uninfected zoster lesions (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oral prednisolone for seven days alongside regular simple analgesia
options.rationale: Corticosteroid alone provides modest acute pain relief without reducing postherpetic neuralgia, and it worsens glycaemic control in a man with diabetes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir for seven days with regular analgesia and review
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy started within 72 hours of rash onset shortens the acute illness and reduces the duration of pain, and adequate early analgesia is itself associated with less postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH).

options.text: Withhold antiviral treatment because he is immunocompetent and review him
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is recommended for all patients over 50 regardless of immune status, because age is the dominant risk factor for postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy for shingles is most effective when started within 72 hours of rash onset, and the indication is strongest in people over 50, those with moderate to severe pain or rash, those with facial or ocular involvement, and the immunocompromised. Beyond 72 hours it is still given where new vesicles are appearing or there is ophthalmic or disseminated disease, since active viral replication continues. Pain control matters in its own right, because poorly controlled acute pain predicts postherpetic neuralgia, which is treated with amitriptyline, gabapentinoids or lignocaine patches. Any involvement of the tip or side of the nose warns of nasociliary branch involvement and requires same day ophthalmology review. Recombinant zoster vaccine is offered after the episode has resolved, and it is funded in Australia for older adults and for defined immunocompromised groups.
key_points: Start antivirals within 72 hours of rash onset wherever possible
Age over 50 is itself an indication for antiviral treatment
Effective early analgesia reduces the risk of postherpetic neuralgia
Lesions on the tip or side of the nose demand urgent eye review
Offer recombinant zoster vaccine after the episode resolves
explanation.pearls: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose, the Hutchinson sign, indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and predict ocular disease, so that finding converts a routine antiviral prescription into a same day ophthalmology referral.
